name: Betavolt BV100 betavoltaic cell
power_basis: electric (maker's claim)
fuel: Nickel-63 foil between diamond semiconductor layers
blurb: Coin-sized nickel-63 battery that trickles power for a claimed 50 years.

name: Plutonium-238 heart pacemaker (Medtronic 9000)
power_basis: thermal (derived from 2.5 Ci of Pu-238; electrical output not verified)
blurb: 1970s heart pacemakers ran for decades on a sliver of plutonium-238.
equivalent: heat equal to ~1/60 of a 5 W phone charger

name: Chicago Pile-1 (first reactor)
power_basis: thermal at first criticality (peaked at 200 W)
fuel: About 5 t of natural uranium metal and 40-45 t of oxide in 330-360 t of graphite
blurb: Fermi's graphite-and-uranium pile in Chicago: the first self-sustaining chain reaction.
equivalent: one-tenth of a 5 W phone charger

name: Soviet Beta-M lighthouse RTG
power_basis: electric when new
blurb: Strontium-90 generators that powered unmanned Soviet Arctic lighthouses and beacons.

name: Apollo ALSEP SNAP-27 RTG
power_basis: electric at start of mission (NASA)
blurb: Astronauts loaded its fuel by hand; it powered Apollo's Moon experiments for years.

name: Perseverance rover MMRTG
power_basis: electric at launch
blurb: Plutonium heat keeps Perseverance and Curiosity running through Martian nights and dust.
equivalent: eleven 10 W LED bulbs (9% of a US home's average draw)

name: Voyager MHW-RTG (one of three per probe)
power_basis: electric per unit at start of mission
fuel: Pu-238 oxide, about 4.5 kg per unit
blurb: Three per Voyager; still powering both probes in interstellar space 49 years on.
equivalent: about sixteen 10 W LED bulbs per generator

name: SNAP-10A (only US reactor flown in space)
power_basis: electric, design minimum (peaked at 590 W)
fuel: Uranium-zirconium hydride, 37 fuel rods; NaK coolant
blurb: The only fission reactor the US has launched; ran 43 days in 1965.

name: NASA Kilopower / KRUSTY test reactor
power_basis: electric, 1 kWe design point (family scales to 10 kWe)
fuel: Cast uranium-molybdenum alloy core, 28 kg U-235; Stirling engines
blurb: NASA's space-reactor prototype, with a core the size of a paper-towel roll.

name: Oklo natural reactor (Gabon)
power_basis: thermal, upper bound (average probably below 100 kW)
fuel: Uranium ore moderated by groundwater; ~5 t of U-235 consumed across 16 zones
blurb: Nature's own reactors pulsed in Gabon uranium ore about two billion years ago.

name: Reed College TRIGA Mark I research reactor
power_basis: thermal, licence limit
blurb: A pool reactor at a liberal-arts college, run mostly by licensed undergraduates.

name: Project Pele mobile microreactor (BWXT)
power_basis: electric (design)
blurb: US military microreactor that ships in four 20-foot containers; now being assembled.

name: USS Nautilus S2W (first nuclear submarine)
power_basis: shaft power (13,400 shp)
blurb: First nuclear submarine; signalled 'underway on nuclear power' in January 1955.

name: Virginia-class submarine S9G reactor
power_basis: shaft power (40,000 shp); reactor ~210 MWt is a public estimate
fuel: Life-of-ship core, no refuelling in ~33 years
blurb: One reactor core lasts this attack submarine's entire 33-year life.

name: Arktika-class icebreaker (2 x RITM-200)
power_basis: shaft power (3 x 20 MW); reactors 2 x 175 MWt
blurb: Twin reactors push this Russian icebreaker through ice 2.8 metres thick.

name: Akademik Lomonosov floating plant (2 x KLT-40S)
power_basis: gross electric (2 x 35 MWe; 32 MWe net each)
blurb: A floating nuclear plant moored at Pevek, the world's northernmost.

name: NuScale Power Module (US460)
power_basis: gross electric per module (~73.5 MWe net)
fuel: Standard PWR fuel, refuelled every two years
blurb: First small modular reactor design approved by US regulators; none built yet.

name: HTR-PM pebble-bed plant (Shidao Bay, China)
power_basis: gross electric, design (two 250 MWt reactors, one turbine); WNA lists 150 MWe net today
blurb: Two helium-cooled pebble-bed reactors share one turbine; in commercial service since 2023.

name: Gerald R. Ford-class carrier (2 x A1B)
power_basis: shaft power, public estimate (US Navy publishes no ratings); reactors ~700 MWt each, inferred
blurb: Two reactors drive a 100,000-ton, 333-metre aircraft carrier at over 30 knots.

name: GE Vernova Hitachi BWRX-300 (Darlington)
power_basis: electric (design)
fuel: 240 GNF2 boiling-water fuel bundles; natural circulation
blurb: A 300 MWe boiling-water SMR now under construction at Darlington, Ontario.

name: Westinghouse AP1000 (Vogtle Unit 3)
power_basis: net electric (1,250 MWe gross)
blurb: America's newest reactors: twin AP1000s at Vogtle, online in 2023 and 2024.

name: EPR (Taishan Unit 1, China)
power_basis: net electric (1,750 MWe gross)
blurb: The most powerful single reactors on Earth: twin EPRs in Guangdong.
equivalent: average draw of ~1.3 million US homes

name: Plant Vogtle (4 units, Georgia, USA)
power_basis: net electric, four units (1,150 + 1,152 + 2 x 1,117)
fuel: Two Westinghouse 4-loop PWRs and two AP1000s
blurb: Largest nuclear plant in the United States: four reactors in Georgia.
equivalent: average draw of ~3.7 million US homes

name: Kashiwazaki-Kariwa (7 units, Japan)
power_basis: net electric nameplate, seven units (5 x 1,067 + 2 x 1,315); 8,212 MWe gross
fuel: Five BWR-5 and two ABWR units
blurb: Long called the world's largest plant; only one of seven units has restarted.
equivalent: average draw of ~6.5 million US homes if all seven units ran

name: Hanul + Shin-Hanul (8 units, South Korea)
power_basis: net electric, eight operable units (Hanul 1-6 = 5,871; Shin-Hanul 1-2 = 2,845)
fuel: Six ~1,000 MWe PWRs and two APR-1400s
blurb: Eight Korean reactors on one coast: the largest nuclear site actually running.
equivalent: average draw of ~7.1 million US homes

name: Every power reactor on Earth
power_basis: net electric, all operable reactors
blurb: All 444 operable power reactors, in 31 countries, added together.
equivalent: average draw of ~330 million US homes
